Caribbean Literature. The literary traditions of the Caribbean islands and mainland territories shaped by a shared history of colonialism, slavery, plantation economy, and postcolonial nation-building. Born from the linguistic, cultural, and spiritual collision of indigenous, African, and European peoples, Caribbean writers explore themes of identity, displacement, hybridity, and resistance.

Colonial powers—Spain, Britain, France, and the Netherlands—extracted wealth through slavery and plantation agriculture, establishing economic and linguistic hierarchies that persist in literature and society. This history is inseparable from contemporary Caribbean writing. Caribbean writers inherited European literary forms like the novel and poetry while wrestling with the question of authentic cultural expression in colonizer languages. Writing in English, French, or Spanish carries the burden of colonial imposition.

Yet the oral storytelling traditions of African diaspora communities and indigenous Caribbean peoples remain vital sources for contemporary writers. These traditions survived slavery and colonialism as acts of cultural preservation. Creole languages—blended, dynamic, and politically charged—appear in Caribbean literature as markers of identity and resistance to colonial erasure. Using creole in literature asserts linguistic sovereignty.

Magical realism and mythological frameworks allow Caribbean writers to honor non-Western epistemologies and to represent histories of trauma and resilience. The marvelous becomes a way of telling truths that realism cannot contain. Major figures include Derek Walcott, Jamaica Kincaid, Edwidge Danticat, and Junot Díaz, whose work ranges from lyric poetry to speculative fiction, articulating postcolonial consciousness and diasporic experience.
